terms.comment: A Celtic word for the aurochs, the wild ox of the German forests, which Caesar describes; Traupman uses it for the buffalo. It is not the same animal.

terms.gloss: buffalo, wild ox; properly an African antelope
terms.comment: Properly a kind of African antelope, but already used in antiquity for the wild ox: Pliny censures the use (NH 8.38), Martial has it. A later form is būfalus (Venantius Fortunatus; Lewis & Short), from which the modern word buffalo comes.

sources: Lewis & Short: urus
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency.
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, in the house spelling; they have not been checked against a modern edition.
